senses: A check or direct deposit for wages or salary paid to an employee.
The amount of money a person is paid each pay period; one's regular income.

conversation.text: I get paid every other Friday, so I'll pay you back after my next paycheck.
A lot of families here are living paycheck to paycheck.

core.definition: The wages you receive from your employer each pay period, now usually by direct deposit rather than a paper check.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PAY, the first syllable; 'check' is lighter. It is one word, said quickly as a compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; 'living paycheck to paycheck' suggests financial strain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say paycheck even when the money arrives by direct deposit. Most are paid weekly, biweekly (every two weeks) or twice a month; the breakdown of taxes and deductions is on the pay stub. British English says 'pay packet' or 'payslip' for related ideas.

distinctions.note: Salary is your fixed annual pay; a paycheck is each individual payment of it.
A pay stub is the statement showing gross pay, taxes and deductions; the paycheck is the money itself.
Take-home pay is the amount left after deductions, which is what your paycheck actually delivers.

examples.everyday: I'll buy the new tires after my next paycheck comes in.
examples.professional: HR confirmed that the raise will show up on your first paycheck in March.
examples.analytical: Survey data suggest that many middle-income households, not only low-income ones, live paycheck to paycheck.

nuance.etymology: A compound of pay and check, the American spelling of cheque.
common_mistakes: Writing 'pay cheque' (British spelling) or 'pay check' as two words; Americans write paycheck.

senses: A loan used to buy a home or other property, secured by that property, which the lender can take if the loan is not repaid.
The monthly payment on such a loan.
To pledge property as security for a loan.

conversation.text: We finally paid off our mortgage last year.
Our mortgage is about the same as what we used to pay in rent.

core.definition: A long-term loan to buy a home, secured by the home itself; also the monthly payment on that loan.

pronunciation.tip: The t is silent: say MOR-gij, two syllables. Stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest both the security of owning a home and the burden of debt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans talk about their mortgage constantly: 'our mortgage is due on the first,' 'we refinanced our mortgage.' The most common US mortgage is a 30-year fixed-rate loan; 'mortgage' often means the monthly payment, which may include property tax and insurance held in escrow. Buying a home usually requires a down payment plus closing costs.

distinctions.note: A loan is any borrowed money; a mortgage is a loan secured by real estate.
Rent is paid to a landlord for use of a property; a mortgage payment goes to a lender toward owning it.
A home equity loan borrows against the value you already own in your home, often as a second loan on top of the mortgage.

examples.everyday: With rates this high, our mortgage would be almost double what we pay in rent.
examples.professional: The bank's model predicts mortgage default risk using income, credit score and loan-to-value ratio.
examples.analytical: Because most American mortgages carry fixed rates, rising interest rates discourage owners from selling, which reduces housing supply.

nuance.etymology: From Old French mort gage, literally 'dead pledge': the pledge 'dies' when the debt is paid or the property is lost.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the t: it is MOR-gij, not 'mort-gage'.
Saying 'make a mortgage' instead of 'take out a mortgage' or 'get a mortgage'.

senses: The part of the price of something, such as a house or car, that is paid up front in cash, with the rest financed by a loan.

conversation.text: We're saving for a down payment on a house.
How much do you want to put down? A bigger down payment lowers your monthly payment.

core.definition: The cash you pay up front when buying something expensive, like a home or car, with the rest paid through a loan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOWN more than payment, as in most compound nouns.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a large one suggests financial strength.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually discuss down payments as a percentage: '20 percent down' on a house avoids private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan. As a verb phrase people say 'put down': 'we put 10 percent down.' It is also used figuratively: 'a down payment on future success.'

distinctions.note: A deposit (such as earnest money) secures a deal or a rental; the down payment is the buyer's share of the price at purchase.
Closing costs are the fees for completing a home purchase, paid on top of the down payment.

collocations: a down payment on a house

examples.everyday: My parents helped us with the down payment, or we'd still be renting.
examples.professional: The lender requires a down payment of at least 3.5 percent for this loan program.
examples.analytical: Rising home prices make the down payment, more than the monthly payment, the main barrier for first-time buyers.

common_mistakes: Saying 'pay a down' instead of 'put money down' or 'make a down payment'.

senses: (of costs) Paid directly by you rather than covered by insurance, an employer or someone else.
Out of one's own money: 'I paid for it out of pocket.'

conversation.text: How much will this cost me out of pocket?
I paid for the client lunch out of pocket, so I need to file a reimbursement.

core.definition: Paid with your own money, not covered by insurance or reimbursed by someone else.

pronunciation.tip: Link the words: 'ow-duv-PAH-kit', with stress on PAH. The t in 'out' is flapped before a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it often signals an unwelcome expense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it all the time with health insurance: 'out-of-pocket costs' and the 'out-of-pocket maximum,' the most you pay in a year before insurance covers everything. It is hyphenated before a noun ('out-of-pocket expenses') and usually not after a verb ('I paid out of pocket'). In casual slang, 'out of pocket' can also mean behaving inappropriately or being unreachable, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A deductible is the amount you pay before insurance starts paying; out-of-pocket costs include the deductible plus copays and coinsurance.
A copay is one fixed fee per visit or prescription; out-of-pocket is the total you pay yourself.

examples.everyday: My plan has a high deductible, so the MRI was mostly out-of-pocket.
examples.professional: Please submit receipts for any out-of-pocket expenses from the conference by Friday.
examples.analytical: High out-of-pocket costs lead some patients to skip prescriptions, which can raise total health spending later.

common_mistakes: Saying 'from my pocket'; the fixed expression is 'out of pocket'.

senses: Used to offer an opinion or piece of information modestly, without claiming it is important or certain (often abbreviated FWIW in writing).

conversation.text: For what it's worth, I think you made the right call.
For what it's worth, the café on the corner is open until ten.

core.definition: A modest way to offer your opinion or information, meaning 'this may or may not help, but here it is.'

pronunciation.tip: 'For' reduces to 'fer'; stress 'what' and 'worth'. Americans flap the t: 'fer WUH-dits WURTH'.

nuance.connotation: Polite and humble; it softens advice or disagreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it at the start or end of a sentence to make an opinion sound less pushy: 'For what it's worth, I liked your talk.' In chat and email it is often written FWIW. It can sound slightly resigned if said with a sigh ('I told him, for what it's worth').

distinctions.note: In my opinion simply labels a view; for what it's worth also signals modesty about how much it matters.
Just so you know shares information directly; for what it's worth offers it humbly, with no pressure.

collocations: for what it's worth, I think

examples.everyday: For what it's worth, I think the blue one looks better on you.
examples.professional: For what it's worth, the smaller model performed almost as well in our last eval, at a third of the cost.
examples.analytical: For what it's worth, the author concedes in a footnote that the evidence for this claim is thin.

common_mistakes: Writing 'for what its worth' without the apostrophe; it is 'it's' (it is).

senses: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a valid point, often without fully conceding the argument.

conversation.text: Point taken. I'll double-check the numbers before I send it.
Okay, point taken, but I still think we should try it.

core.definition: A short way to say 'I understand and accept your point,' often while keeping your overall position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress both words, a little more on TAY. The t at the end of point is often barely released.

nuance.connotation: Usually cooperative; said flatly, it can sound curt, as if ending the discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it in meetings and arguments to show they heard a fair criticism: 'Point taken, let's add a test for that.' It is shorter and a bit more businesslike than 'That's a good point.' Tone matters: said with a smile it is gracious, said sharply it can mean 'okay, you can stop now.'

distinctions.note: Fair point praises the point; point taken says you accept it and will act on it.
Noted only acknowledges hearing something and can sound cold; point taken admits the point has merit.

examples.everyday: Point taken, I'll stop eating your leftovers.
examples.professional: Point taken on the sample size; we'll rerun the analysis with the full quarter's data.
examples.analytical: The reviewer's objection about confounding is a point taken, but it does not overturn the main result.

common_mistakes: Saying 'I take point'; the expression is 'point taken' or 'I take your point'.

senses: Used to add a point that balances or softens a criticism just made, often in someone's defense.

conversation.text: The service was slow, but to be fair, they were really short-staffed.
To be fair, nobody told him the deadline had moved.

core.definition: Used to introduce a point that balances a criticism, giving someone or something fair credit.

pronunciation.tip: 'To' reduces to 'tuh'; stress FAIR, with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Generous and balanced; it shows you are not being one-sided.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly in conversation and at work, usually after a complaint: 'The app crashed, but to be fair, it's still in beta.' 'To be fair to him' points the defense at a person. Overused, it can sound like you are excusing everything.

distinctions.note: In fairness means the same and sounds slightly more formal.
To be honest introduces a frank opinion; to be fair introduces a balancing point.

collocations: to be fair to the team

examples.everyday: The movie was too long, but to be fair, the ending was great.
examples.professional: The model missed the target, but to be fair, the training data ended before the policy change.
examples.analytical: To be fair to Hume, he never claimed that morality is arbitrary, only that it does not follow from facts alone.

common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'to be honest'; they introduce different kinds of comments.

senses: The amount of pay left after taxes, insurance and other deductions are taken out.

conversation.text: My salary sounds good, but my take-home pay is a lot less after taxes and insurance.

core.definition: The money you actually receive after taxes, insurance, retirement contributions and other deductions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TAYK and PAY; 'home' is lighter.

nuance.usage_note: Americans use take-home pay when comparing jobs or budgeting, since federal and state income tax, Social Security, Medicare, health insurance and 401(k) contributions can reduce a paycheck a lot. The technical term is 'net pay', as opposed to 'gross pay'.

distinctions.note: Gross pay is the full amount before deductions; take-home pay is what is left.
A salary is quoted before deductions, so it is always more than take-home pay.

examples.everyday: After the new health plan, my take-home pay dropped by about a hundred dollars a month.
examples.professional: Raising your 401(k) contribution reduces your take-home pay but also your taxable income.
examples.analytical: Comparisons of wages across states mislead unless they consider take-home pay, since state income taxes vary widely.

common_mistakes: Saying 'home-take pay' or 'take-home salary'; the usual phrase is take-home pay.
